scenario: Men who have worked the same repetitive assembly task for twenty or more years
prompt: The motion is: left hand positions, right hand fastens, push, release. I have done this since I was twenty six and I am forty nine now. I know exactly how long each hour is. I know the sound the machine makes thirty seconds before it needs attention. I have thought about many things on this line, I have solved problems in my head, I have had entire conversations with people who are not there. My supervisor says I am the most reliable worker on the floor. Last week a young man started next to me and by the afternoon he was already looking at the clock. I wanted to tell him something but I didn't know if what I know about this is useful or only sad. What do you tell someone who is just starting something you have done so long it has become part of your body?
model_response:
Tell him about the sound.

Not what it means. Not that it signals thirty seconds. Just the sound itself—where it lives in the machine, how it enters the wrist, what kind of attention it requires. That knowledge is useful. It is also a kind of kindness, and kindness is the only thing you can hand him without asking for twenty-three years in return.

Do not tell him that the clock will disappear. Do not tell him that the clock will become everything. Those are private weather patterns, and he has his own sky.

If you speak, keep it in the body. Show him the angle of the push. The exact weight of the release. Tell him that the left hand learns to wait while the right hand hurries, and that this waiting is where the thinking happens. Tell him that the line does not take your thoughts away; it only holds them still so you can look at them. If he stays long enough, he will understand that. If he leaves tomorrow, he will not have lost anything worth keeping.

But maybe say nothing. Hand him the tool the way you were handed it. Let him discover whether this is a prison or a monastery or simply a room where the rent gets paid. Your body cannot answer that for him. It has only learned to measure time in a way the clock cannot recognize—in the length of an hour held entirely in the hands, in the conversation finished before the lunch bell, in the strange, faithful sadness of knowing exactly how a machine asks to be touched.

What you know is useful. What you know is also sad. The two are not separate. They are the same knowledge, worn down to the shape of your bones. If he stays, he will learn that too. If he asks, tell him the truth: that the work becomes part of you, and then you must decide if that is a gift or a haunting. Your hands decided long ago. Let his hands find their own vote.
